units.title: Hello, Dart
units.summary: Write your first Dart program with void main and print, and work with strings and numbers.

lesson.md: Every Dart program starts in a function called `main`. You write it as `void main()`, followed by curly braces `{ }`. The word `void` means that `main` gives back no value. The code between the braces runs from top to bottom.

`print` shows a value and then starts a new line. Text in quotes, like `'Hello'`, is called a **string**. Dart accepts single quotes `'...'` and double quotes `"..."`; this course uses single quotes. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
If you forget a semicolon, Dart reports an error and the program does not run at all. Dart is also case-sensitive: `Print` is not the same as `print`.
Numbers do not need quotes. Dart calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses come first.

The operator `/` always gives a decimal number: `7 / 2` is `3.5`, and `6 / 2` is `3.0`. The operator `~/` divides and drops the rest, so `7 ~/ 2` is `3`. The operator `%` gives the rest of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.
For strings, `+` joins the text: `'2' + '3'` is `23`, not `5`. Inside a string, `\n` starts a new line.
You cannot join a string and a number with `+`: `'Age: ' + 5` is an error. Unit 3 shows how to put numbers into strings.

card: `void main() { }` is where the program starts
`print(x);` shows `x` and starts a new line

exercises.explain: `print` with a small `p` shows the value, and the statement ends with a semicolon. Without `;`, or with `Print` or `echo`, the program does not compile.
`*` comes before `+`: `4 * 2` is `8`, and `3 + 8` is `11`.
`17` divided by `5` is `3` with a rest of `2`. The operator `%` gives the rest.
The operator `/` always gives a decimal number. `10 / 4` is `2.5`.
`'4'` and `'5'` are strings because of the quotes. `+` joins strings, so the result is `45`.
`/` always gives a decimal number, so the program prints `4.0`. Use `8 ~/ 2` to get `4`.

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables with var, final and const, meet int, double, String and bool, and handle null.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. `var count = 3;` creates the variable `count` and stores `3` in it. The `=` stores a value; this is called **assignment**. Later you can store a new value without `var`. `count += 2` adds `2` to the variable, and `count++` adds `1`.

Every value has a **type**. `int` is a whole number, `double` is a number with a decimal part, `String` is text and `bool` is `true` or `false`. With `var`, Dart works out the type from the value. You can also write the type instead of `var`.
A variable keeps its type. After `var count = 3;`, the line `count = 'three';` is an error, because `count` is an `int`.

A `final` variable gets its value only once. A `const` variable also never changes, and its value must be known before the program runs, for example a number written in the code. Use `final` or `const` for every value that does not change.

The value `null` means "no value". Normal types like `int` and `String` can never hold `null`. Add a `?` to the type to allow it: a `String?` holds a string or `null`. A `String?` variable without a value starts as `null`.

`int.tryParse('42')` turns a string into an `int`. If the string is not a number, it gives `null`, so its type is `int?`. Where Dart needs an `int`, you can write `!` after the value: it says "this is not `null`". If the value is `null` after all, the program stops with an error.

card: `var x = 5;` creates a variable, Dart works out the type
`final` is set once, `const` is fixed before the program runs

exercises.explain: `x` starts as `4`, becomes `8` after `x * 2`, and `x += 1` adds `1`: `9`.
`4.5` has a decimal part, so it is a `double`. An `int` holds only whole numbers.
A `final` variable gets its value only once. The line `city = 'Oslo';` is an error, so the program does not run.
A `String?` variable without a value starts as `null`, and `print` shows `null`.

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Put values into strings with $ and ${...}, and use length, toUpperCase, contains and substring.

lesson.md: You can put a variable into a string with `$` and the name: `'Hello, $name!'`. Dart replaces `$name` with the value of `name`. This is called **string interpolation**, and it works with numbers too.

lesson.output:
Hello, Ada!
Ada is 36 years old.

lesson.md: For more than a name, use `${...}` with curly braces. Dart calculates what is inside the braces and puts the result into the string.

A string knows things about itself. `.length` gives the number of characters. A **method** is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot and parentheses: `word.toUpperCase()` gives the string in capital letters, `word.toLowerCase()` in small letters.
`contains` checks whether a string contains another string and gives `true` or `false`. `startsWith` checks the beginning. Capital and small letters count as different.

Every character has a position, called its **index**. Counting starts at `0`, so `word[0]` is the first character. `substring(start, end)` gives the part from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Without `end`, it goes to the end of the string. `indexOf` gives the index where a part first appears.
Strings never change. `word.toUpperCase()` gives a **new** string; `word` itself keeps its value. Store the result if you need it: `var big = word.toUpperCase();`.

card: `'Hi, $name'` puts a variable into a string
`'${a + b}'` puts a result into a string
`s[0]` is the first character, `s.substring(1, 3)` a part

exercises.explain: `$name` is replaced by the value of `name`, which is `Sam`.
Dart calculates `x * 2` inside `${...}`, which is `10`. The `x = ` outside the braces is normal text.
`length` counts the characters: `h`, `e`, `l`, `l`, `o` are `5` characters.
The index starts at `0`. `substring(1, 3)` takes the characters at index `1` and `2`: `a` and `r`.
Capital and small letters count as different. `'Paris'` does not contain `'paris'`, so it prints `false`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program decide with if and else, comparisons, && and ||, switch, the ternary operator and ??.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses, the code in curly braces. The code after `else` runs when the condition is `false`.

Comparison operators give a `bool`: `==` means equal, `!=` not equal, `<` less than, `>` greater than, `<=` less than or equal, `>=` greater than or equal. Do not mix them up: `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values.
With `else if` you check another condition when the one before was `false`. Dart checks from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`.
Logical operators combine conditions: `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`, `||` (or) when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
`switch` compares one value with several `case` labels and runs the code of the matching one. Only that case runs; you do not need `break`. The `default` case runs when no case matches.

The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` gives `a` when the condition is `true`, and `b` otherwise. The operator `??` gives the value on the left, or the value on the right when the left one is `null`.

card: `c ? a : b` picks a value, `x ?? 'none'` replaces `null`

exercises.explain: `7 % 2` is `1`, so `x % 2 == 0` is `false` and the `else` block runs.
`15 > 20` is `false`, `15 > 10` is `true`, so `mild` is printed. After that, Dart skips the rest.

exercises.statement: In Dart, `=` compares two values and `==` stores a value.
exercises.explain: It is the other way round: `=` stores a value in a variable, `==` compares two values.
`5 > 3` is `true`, but `2 > 4` is `false`. `&&` needs both sides to be `true`.

`0 > 0` is `false`, so the ternary operator gives the value after `:`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for, for-in, while and do-while, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats code. `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)` has three parts, separated by semicolons: the start `var i = 0`, the condition `i < 3` that is checked before every round, and the step `i++` that runs after every round.
The step can be anything that changes the variable. `i--` subtracts `1`, `i -= 3` subtracts `3`, and `i *= 2` multiplies by `2`.
`for (var item in items)` runs once for every item of a list, from first to last. A list is written in square brackets, like `['apple', 'pear']`; you learn more about lists in unit 7.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. It checks the condition before every round, so it can also run zero times. Change a variable inside the loop, or the loop never ends.
A `do` ... `while` loop runs its body first and checks the condition after it, so the body runs at least once. Note the semicolon after `while (...)`.
`break` stops the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.

card: `for (var x in items) { }` goes through every item
`while (c) { }` checks first, `do { } while (c);` runs at least once
`break` stops the loop, `continue` goes to the next round

`while` checks the condition first. `5 < 5` is `false`, so the body never runs and only `done` is printed.
A `do` ... `while` loop runs its body before it checks the condition, so `inside` is printed once.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with return types, optional and named parameters, and the short arrow syntax =>.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run as often as you like. You already know `main`. You write your own functions outside of `main`: first the return type, then the name, then the **parameters** in parentheses. `void` means that the function gives back no value.
`return` sends a value back to the code that called the function, and the function ends there. Write the type of that value before the name, for example `int add(int a, int b)`.
When a function only returns one expression, you can use `=>`. `int square(int x) => x * x;` means the same as `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`.
Parameters in square brackets `[ ]` are **optional**. You can leave them out when you call the function. Give them a default value with `=`, which is used when the value is missing.

Parameters in curly braces `{ }` are **named**. When you call the function, you write the name and a colon, like `width: 3`, and the order does not matter. Named parameters are optional, unless you mark them with `required`.
Dart checks the types of the parameters before the program runs. `add('2', 3)` is an error, because `add` needs two `int` values.

`int square(int x) => x * x;` for one expression

units.title: Collections
units.summary: Keep many values in a List, a Map or a Set, change them, and transform lists with map and where.

lesson.md: A **List** holds many values in a fixed order. You write it in square brackets `[ ]`, with commas between the values. `List<String>` means a list of strings. `names[0]` is the first item, because the index starts at `0`. `.length` gives the number of items, and `.last` the last item.
`add` puts a value at the end of a list. `list[i] = value` replaces an item, and `remove` takes a value out. `contains` checks whether a value is in the list.

You can go through a list with a for-in loop. `map` makes a new value from every item, and `where` keeps only the items for which a condition is `true`. Both take a short function, like `(n) => n * 2`. Add `.toList()` to get a list again.

A **Map** stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**, in curly braces: `{'apple': 3}`. `stock['apple']` reads the value for a key; a missing key gives `null`. Assigning to a key adds or changes a pair. `<String, int>{}` is an empty map with `String` keys and `int` values.
`.keys` gives all keys and `.values` all values; `print` shows them in round brackets. To go through the pairs, loop over `.entries`; every entry has a `key` and a `value`.

A **Set** holds every value only once. You write it in curly braces with values only: `{'dart', 'code'}`. Adding a value that is already in the set changes nothing. An empty `{}` is a map, so write `<String>{}` for an empty set.

The key `'coffee'` is not in the map, so reading it gives `null`.
A set holds every value once. Adding `2` again changes nothing, so the set is `{1, 2, 3}` with `3` values.

units.title: Classes
units.summary: Build your own types with classes: fields, constructors with this., methods, getters and toString.

lesson.md: A **class** is a plan for your own type. It describes data, called **fields**, and actions, called **methods**. A value made from a class is an **object**. `Dog()` creates a new object of the class `Dog`. You reach its fields and methods with a dot.

A **constructor** sets the fields when an object is created. It has the same name as the class. `Point(this.x, this.y);` takes two values and stores them in the fields `x` and `y`. The word `this` means the object itself. Fields that never change can be `final`.
A constructor can also have named parameters, like a function: `Person({required this.name, this.age = 0});`. The caller writes the names, and missing values use their default.
A **getter** looks like a field, but it calculates its value every time you read it. Write `get` before the name and no parentheses. You also read it without parentheses: `r.area`.

When you print an object, Dart calls its method `toString`. Without your own version, it prints `Instance of 'Point'`. You write your own `toString` with `@override` in front; `@override` says that you replace a method that every class already has.
